item.title: AWS releases official local emulator for cloud services
item.description:
AWS releases official local emulator for cloud services

On 11 November 2026 AWS released an official emulator that lets developers run a local clone of many AWS services without needing a paid API key.

🔍 Overview

  • Official emulator from AWS.
  • Provides a local clone of many different services.
  • Eliminates the need for a paid API key during testing.

🧩 How it works

  • Implemented in Rust.
  • Distributed as a Docker image; currently requires Docker on macOS or Windows.
  • Runs services locally, enabling tests against the emulator.

⚙️ Key details

  • 29,684 commits in the first three weeks of the project.
  • Developed by a huge swarm of agents.
  • Swaminathan (Swami) Sivasubramanian described its origin in a guest post on Werner Vogels’ blog.

🚀 Availability

  • Announced 11 November 2026 (Link Blog).
  • Requires Docker; a single‑binary distribution is hoped for in the future.

💡 Why it matters

  • Allows testing without provisioning paid AWS resources.
  • Can speed development cycles and reduce costs.

#AWS #Emulator #Rust

Source: aws-emulator

item.title: Claude Opus 5.5 Optimizes SQLite C Extension Performance Beyond Rust Implementation
item.description:
Claude Opus 5.5 Optimizes SQLite C Extension Performance Beyond Rust Implementation

On November 8th, 2026, an investigation using the Claude Opus 5.5 model demonstrated the creation and optimization of a custom SQLite extension. The project focused on developing a parse_number() function to convert strings—such as currency and percentages—into numeric values that can be summed and sorted.

🔍 Overview

The parse_number(value) function was designed with specific parsing capabilities:

  • Strips symbols including ‘,’, ‘$’, ‘£’, and ‘%’.
  • Handles leading ‘-’ characters.
  • Returns ‘NULL’ for any values it cannot successfully parse.

⚙️ Key details

The development process compared building the extension in C versus Rust, revealing significant differences in file size and execution speed:

  • File Size: The C extension resulted in a 14 KB file, while Rust implementations were significantly larger at 321 KB (using Rusqlite) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs).
  • Performance Optimization: Although the Rust version was initially faster due to its strtod equivalent being twice as fast as C’s, a custom C function written by the AI achieved superior speeds.

📊 Performance results

The following table displays the net cost per row measured over 2 million rows. Lower values indicate better performance.

Data Type Original C New C Rusqlite (Rust) sqlite-loadable (Rust)
Mixed data 67 ns 19 ns 46 ns 41 ns
Integers only 25 ns 16 ns 36 ns 32 ns
Decimals only 106 ns 18 ns 55 ns 47 ns

🚀 Availability

The final prototype was formatted as a research report for the simonw/research GitHub repository. The model provided the investigation as a downloadable zip file containing the necessary folder structure for the repository.

#SQLite #ClaudeAI #Programming #Rust #C

Source: Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust

item.title: Proof‑Driven Development introduced with PDD Kit and Verus for Rust
item.description:
Proof‑Driven Development introduced with PDD Kit and Verus for Rust

Proof‑Driven Development (PDD) arrives as a new software‑development paradigm supported by PDD Kit. The toolkit helps teams turn their intent into formal specifications, automatically proves the generated code for every input, and falls back to tests when a proof cannot reach.

🔍 Overview

  • Coding agents can now generate whole features that span tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code.
  • Traditional line‑by‑line review does not scale to this output, and tests often only check what the agent built, not what was originally requested.
  • A plan is meant to be the contract between a developer and an agent, but the agent is not forced to obey it, leading to hidden gaps that surface only as bug reports or edge‑case failures.

🧩 How it works

  1. Intent → Formal Spec – PDD Kit works with you to express the parts of your intent that can be formalized as a specification in Verus.
  2. Proof Generation – The kit automatically generates a mathematical proof that the agent’s code satisfies the formal spec for every possible input.
  3. Fallback to Tests – Anything the proof cannot reach (e.g., third‑party cryptography libraries, UI code) is turned into informal specifications and covered by high‑quality unit, end‑to‑end, terminal‑automation, and browser‑automation tests.
  4. TCB Sign‑off – The boundary between proved code and tested code is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB). PDD Kit makes this line explicit and asks the developer to sign off on each piece.
  5. Collaboration Environment – The workflow runs inside GitHub Next’s Chopin, a real‑time, multiplayer planning environment where teams and agents can co‑author a shared document.

⚙️ Key details

  • PDD Kit – the toolkit that drives the Proof‑Driven Development process.
  • Verus – the verifier used today; a proof language for Rust co‑developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI‑SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison, and the Weizmann Institute of Science.
  • Chopin – the planning interface that lets a team and agents iterate on the plan and proposed tests before handing off implementation.
  • Formal verification – a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every input, providing stronger assurance than testing alone.
  • Evidence vs. Proof – a passing test is labeled as evidence; only a verifier‑checked proof guarantees correctness for all inputs.
  • Real‑world case – inside Chopin, PDD Kit was used to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust storefront. Verus hardened the code, uncovered existing bugs, and proved the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification.

💡 Why it matters

  • Proofs cover the entire input space, catching bugs that a test suite—no matter how large—might miss.
  • By making the TCB explicit, teams understand exactly which pieces rely on trust and can review them separately.
  • The approach scales to agent‑generated code where traditional code review is infeasible.
  • It bridges the gap between the plan (the contract) and the shipped code, reducing the hidden mismatch that typically appears only after deployment.

📊 Components at a glance

Component Role
PDD Kit Turns intent into formal specs, generates proofs and tests
Verus Verifier that checks Rust code against formal specs
Chopin (GitHub Next) Real‑time, multiplayer planning environment for teams and agents

#ProofDrivenDevelopment #FormalVerification #AIcodingAgents #Rust

Source: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit - Microsoft Research

item.title: Rust‑Based docling.rs Speeds Up Document Conversion for LLM Pipelines
item.description:
Rust‑Based docling.rs Speeds Up Document Conversion for LLM Pipelines

The docling.rs project released a Rust port of IBM’s docling that delivers faster, lower‑memory document conversion for LLM and RAG pipelines.

🔧 Overview

  • Converts PDF, Office, HTML, scanned documents, and audio into Markdown, docling JSON, and other formats that LLMs or RAG pipelines can consume.
  • Produces output that is byte‑for‑byte identical to the original IBM docling implementation.
  • Operates as a single static binary – no Python runtime and no PyTorch dependency.

⚙️ How it works

  • Layout analysis, table recognition, and OCR are performed by built‑in ONNX models (layout, OCR, TableFormer, Whisper). These models are bundled (under 1 GB) and can be downloaded once via the provided scripts.
  • Office, HTML, Markdown, and e‑mail formats require no ML models.
  • PDF, images, and audio trigger the ONNX models for full‑fidelity extraction.

🚀 Performance

Format Speedup vs. Python docling RAM usage
PDF 4.3× faster under half
Office & HTML 20–60× faster —
  • Table extraction retains structure with cell recall 0.94, compared to MarkItDown’s 0.31 (see numbers).

🔗 Compatibility with existing stacks

  • MarkItDown: pip install docling-rs and replace the import with from docling_rs.markitdown import MarkItDown. All original formats, layout analysis, tables, and OCR remain functional.
  • Marker: Swap imports to from docling_rs.marker.converters.pdf import PdfConverter and keep the original API (create_model_dict, text_from_rendered, JSON block tree, etc.).
  • MinerU: Replace imports to from docling_rs.mineru.parser import parse and retain MinerU 4’s SDK (ParseResult, markdown(), JSON, Content Lists, save()).
  • Each compatibility guide includes side‑by‑side measurements (MarkItDown, Marker, MinerU).

🌐 Availability

  • Install with pip: pip install docling-rs.
  • Install with npm or from source checkout.
  • Download models once with: 
    1
2

    import docling_rs
docling_rs.download_models()
    or via download_dependencies.sh for non‑Python workflows.
  • Windows support documented in docs/WINDOWS.md.
  • Try the converter directly in the browser (WebAssembly, OCR included) at https://docling-project.github.io/docling.rs/ – processing stays on your device.

📚 Documentation

  • Detailed performance and profiling notes: ./docs/PDF_CONFORMANCE.md#performance--review--profiling-notes.
  • Model download instructions: see the Getting the ML models section referenced in the docs.
  • API migration guides for MarkItDown, Marker, and MinerU are linked in each bullet above.

#docling #Rust #documentconversion #LLM #RAG

Source: docling-project/docling.rs

item.title: Claw Code: Rust‑Based Agent‑Managed Museum Exhibit Using Gajae‑Code and LazyCodex
item.description:
Claw Code: Rust‑Based Agent‑Managed Museum Exhibit Using Gajae‑Code and LazyCodex

An agent-managed museum exhibit called Claw Code has been released. It is a public Rust implementation of the claw CLI agent harness, built with the Gajae-Code and LazyCodex toolchains and designed to run without any human intervention.

🔍 Overview

  • The repository is described as a museum exhibit rather than a commercial product.
  • It is “closer to a museum exhibit than a product pitch,” kept alive by “crab‑run” artifact processes and automatically maintained by agents.
  • The project philosophy explicitly states it is not meant to be hand‑operated like a normal product repo.

🛠️ How It Works

  • The exhibit is agent‑managed: harnesses plan, execute, verify, label, and preserve the artifact while “crabs keep the tank running.”
  • The canonical source lives in the rust/ directory, with the current source of truth being ultraworkers/claw-code.
  • claw is the CLI agent harness; Claw Code provides its public Rust implementation.

📦 Getting Started

  • Start with LazyCodex or Gajae‑Code if you want to run work.
  • For build, authentication, CLI usage, session handling, and parity‑harness workflows, consult USAGE.md.
  • After building, run claw doctor as the first health check.
  • Detailed crate information is in rust/README.md; the Rust‑port checkpoint is documented in PARITY.md.
  • Container‑first workflow instructions are in docs/container.md.
  • Windows users can follow the PowerShell‑first quickstart in docs/windows-install-release.md.
  • For file submission or navigation questions, see docs/navigation-file-context.md.
  • Setup for local OpenAI‑compatible models and offline skill installs is covered in docs/local-openai-compatible-providers.md.

📡 Integration & Status

  • ACP / Zed: Claw Code does not ship an ACP/Zed daemon or JSON‑RPC entrypoint yet.
  • Use claw acp (or claw --acp) to query the current status; claw acp serve is a discoverability alias that returns status with exit code 0.
  • Real ACP support remains tracked in ROADMAP.md.
  • The public JSON contract is defined in docs/g011-acp-json-rpc-status-contract.md.

🚀 Availability & Community

  • Repository: ultraworkers/claw-code (GitHub).
  • Join the development discussion on Discord:
    • Harness Lab – Discord‑join the harness lab
    • Crab Tank – Discord‑join the crab tank
  • Star history for the repository is publicly visible.
  • For a longer public explanation of the project philosophy, see the linked tweet in the source material.

All details are drawn directly from the project documentation and announcements.

#Rust #AIagents #AgentManagement #OpenSource

Source: ultraworkers/claw-code

item.title: jcode: High-Performance Rust Coding Agent Harness Update
item.description:
jcode: High-Performance Rust Coding Agent Harness Update

The jcode coding agent harness, written in Rust, has received an update that improves performance, resource efficiency, and its update workflow.

🔍 Overview

  • High performance coding agent harness written in Rust.
  • Described as the most RAM-efficient and most intelligent harness.

🛠️ Features

  • Offers Homebrew installation, source builds, and provider setup options.
  • Can be driven via a TUI or terminal commands.

⚙️ Update Mechanics

  • In the TUI, run /update to download the latest stable release in the background and reload while preserving the session.
  • From the terminal, execute jcode update then restart the client.
  • Both commands share the same update policy, also applied to development builds.
  • Updates skip older or equal release versions.
  • For dev builds, the running binary’s Git commit is compared with the release tag; builds ahead of, identical to, or diverged from the release are preserved.
  • If ancestry cannot be verified locally or via GitHub, the update stops to avoid a downgrade.
  • The dev patch includes a commit‑count offset and is not used for release version comparison.
  • Default behavior uses features.update_channel = "stable". An explicit "main" channel opts into source‑branch updates.
  • Use /rebuild or the self-dev build workflow to rebuild a checkout.

📊 Performance Metrics

Tool RAM Usage (MB) Relative to jcode
jcode (local embedding off) 27.8 baseline
jcode 167.1 6.0×
pi 144.4 5.2×
Codex CLI 140.0 5.0×
OpenCode 371.5 13.4×
GitHub Copilot CLI 333.3 12.0×
Cursor Agent 214.9 7.7×
Claude Code 386.6 13.9×
Antigravity CLI 243.7 8.8×

🚀 Availability

  • Installation can be performed via Homebrew, source builds, or provider setup.
  • An agent can perform the setup for you.

item.title: Introduction of tokenizers v1 with SIMD and Parallelism Improvements
item.description:
Introduction of tokenizers v1 with SIMD and Parallelism Improvements

A new version of the tokenizers library, v1, has been released. The goal of this version was to improve performance while preserving the API, vocabulary, merge ranks, and output of v0.23, ensuring v1 produces the same token IDs as the previous version.

🧩 How it works

Tokenizers run conversions in four stages:

Stage Description
Normalization Applies operations such as Unicode normalization or lowercasing to raw text.
Pre-tokenization Splits text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens.
Model Maps each pre-token to IDs in its vocabulary.
Post-processing Adds special tokens expected by the model.

⚙️ Key details

BPE and Model Support

  • The library supports three model types: Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), WordPiece, and Unigram.
  • Eight of the ten measured model families use BPE.
  • BPE models use regular expressions to split input text into pre-tokens; merges occur inside a pre-token and never across boundaries.

Performance Optimizations

  • SIMD Instructions: For a handful of common grammars, a hand-written function uses SIMD instructions to find splits via boolean operations over bitstreams instead of a regex engine. This process, using bitcannon, views input bytes as parallel streams and decides 64 bytes per register operation.
  • Memory Management: The merge working set uses a caller-owned scratch buffer to avoid touching the allocator. Merged pieces form an intrusive doubly-linked list inside one preallocated buffer, allowing merges to update two indices rather than moving data.
  • Caching: A thread-local memo maps pre-token bytes to finished IDs, allowing repeated words to be merged once.
  • Concurrency: Each thread draws its scratch buffer and word cache from its own sub-pool, allowing one shared tokenizer to encode from many threads at once without queuing on a single lock.

Architecture Changes

  • The library remains general across tokenizer families and loads everything v0.23 loaded.
  • The project structure moved from one crate to a workspace:
    • tk-encode: The required runtime.
    • tk-serialize, tk-convert, and tk-train: Linked only when an application needs them.

#tokenizers #BPE #SIMD #NLP #Rust

Source: tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

item.title: Targeted Attacks Against Rust Developers and Crate Owners
item.description:
Targeted Attacks Against Rust Developers and Crate Owners

Adam Harvey and the crates security team have issued a warning regarding an ongoing campaign targeting rust-lang members and owners of popular crates to compromise devices and accounts for the purpose of publishing malware.

🧩 How it works

Attackers use video calls framed as positive opportunities—such as projects, jobs, or contract opportunities—as a vector to:

  • Get the target to install software on their computer (e.g., a purportedly missing audio codec).
  • Get the target to execute a command (e.g., via a command placed on the clipboard).

⚙️ Key details

  • Impact: Last month, this method was used in a successful supply chain attack against the array ref crate and others.
  • Risk Factor: Every piece of software depending on open source has a network of human beings who are potential attack vectors, specifically anyone with publishing rights to packages in the dependency network.
  • Defense: A recommended defense is the use of dependency cooldowns, which involves waiting a few days before upgrading to new package releases to allow others to spot supply chain attacks.

#Rust #Cybersecurity #SupplyChainAttack #OpenSource

Source: Be alert: targeted attacks on prominent Rustaceans

item.title: AI Agent Skill Translates CUDA Tile Kernels to cuTile Rust
item.description:
AI Agent Skill Translates CUDA Tile Kernels to cuTile Rust

A new AI agent skill has been developed to translate GPU kernels from cuTile Python and Triton-TileIR into cuTile Rust, a tile-based system designed for safe and idiomatic GPU kernel authoring in the Rust programming language.

🔍 Overview

cuTile Rust extends the Rust ownership model to tile-based GPU kernels by splitting mutable outputs into disjoint pieces and preserving the host-side ownership contract across kernel launches. It serves as one of three front ends—alongside cuTile Python and Triton-TileIR—that feed into the same CUDA Tile IR (the cuda_tile dialect) and the tileiras compiler, which emits the GPU binary.

🧩 How it works

The translation process uses a bounded multi-agent pipeline that covers the following stages:

  • Analysis
  • Device kernel creation
  • Host and FFI code generation
  • Benchmarking

Each stage concludes with a machine-checkable verdict. Because all three front ends share the same IR, translation is verified by “diffing” the Tile IR of the reference kernel and the translated kernel to ensure they reproduce the same reductions, tile shapes, and memory-op families before tests are executed.

⚙️ Key details

There are significant differences between the JIT compilation of cuTile Python and the ahead-of-time compilation of Rust source:

  • Specialization: cuTile Python specializes kernels implicitly at call time. In contrast, cuTile Rust requires every specialization to be declared in the kernel’s signature; nothing is specialized unless declared.
  • Structural Changes: A single Python kernel may become multiple Rust entries. For example, layer_norm splits into 2-Dnchw and 1-Dw1 entries because the branch changes tile rank.
  • Compilation: Rust source is compiled ahead of time, with tile shapes and element types checked by rustc. The crate embeds the kernel AST, and the runtime specializes it with concrete const-generic values to compile a cached cubin at first launch.
  • ABI Support: Supporting a dtype is an explicit ABI extension. Supported types include sf32, f16, bf16, i32, i64, f8e5m2, and f8e4m3fn.

🚀 Availability

The translation skill is shipped in the TileGym repo. In TileGym, cuTile Rust functions as a backend that can be activated using tilegym.set_backend("cutile-rs") to route the operator API to Rust kernels.

💡 Why it matters

Using this AI agent skill, all 24 public TileGym operators—comprising roughly 40 GPU kernels—were ported to cuTile Rust. These kernels range from element-wise operations to mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), and flash-attention decode. On average, the ported kernels reached 99.5% of cuTile Python performance.

#Rust #CUDA #GPU #AIagents #TileGym

Source: Translating CUDA Tile Operations from Python to Rust Using Agentic AI | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: SpaceXAI releases Grok Build: a terminal-based AI coding agent
item.description:
SpaceXAI releases Grok Build: a terminal-based AI coding agent

SpaceXAI has open‑sourced Grok Build, its terminal‑based AI coding agent.

🔍 Overview

  • Grok Build is a terminal‑based AI coding agent developed by SpaceXAI.
  • It runs as a full‑screen text user interface (TUI) that can understand a codebase, edit files, execute shell commands, search the web, and manage long‑running tasks.
  • It can be used interactively, headlessly for scripting/CI, or embedded in editors via the Agent Client Protocol (ACP).

🛠️ How it works

  • The repository contains the Rust source for the grok CLI/TUI and its agent runtime.
  • The source tree is synced periodically from the SpaceXAI monorepo; a SOURCE_REV file records the exact monorepo commit SHA.
  • The workspace Cargo.toml is generated and should be treated as read‑only.
  • Build requirements:
    • Rust toolchain pinned by rust-toolchain.toml; rustup installs automatically on first build.
    • DotSlash is required so hermetic tools under bin/ (e.g., bin/protoc) can be downloaded and run; ensure dotslash is on your PATH before building.
    • protoc proto codegen resolves bin/protoc via DotSlash or falls back to a protoc on PATH / $PROTOC.

⚙️ Key details

  • Supported build hosts: macOS and Linux; Windows builds are best‑effort and not currently tested from this tree.
  • Prebuilt binaries are published for macOS, Linux, and Windows.
  • The binary artifact is named xai-grok-pager; official installs ship it as grok.
  • On first launch the tool opens a browser for authentication (see the authentication guide).
  • Full online documentation: https://docs.x.ai/build/overview
  • User guide location: crates/codegen/xai-grok-pager/docs/user-guide/ (covers getting started, keyboard shortcuts, slash commands, configuration, theming, MCP servers, skills, plugins, hooks, headless mode, sandboxing, and more).

📦 Availability

  • Releases include a changelog with fixes, features, and improvements: https://x.ai/build/changelog
  • Binaries can be downloaded for the three major platforms.

📄 Licensing

  • First‑party code in the repository is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0.
  • Third‑party and vendored code retains its original licenses.
  • External contributions are not accepted.

#SpaceXAI #AIcoding #Rust #TerminalAI

Source: xai-org/grok-build
